   171	\section{Finite fields, traces, and self-dual bases}
   172	% Paper labels sec:finite-fields, sec:subfields, sec:ff-representations kept
   173	% for cross-reference fidelity.
   174	\label{sec:finite-fields}
   175	\label{sec:subfields}
   176	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   177	
   178	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ a prime power. We write $\F_p$ and $\F_q$ for
   179	the finite fields with $p$ and $q$ elements; $p$ is the characteristic of
   180	$\F_q$, and $\F_p$ is its prime subfield.
   181	
   182	\begin{definition}[Coordinate map and multiplication tables]\label{def:subfields-kappa}
   183		% The source lets k range over all integers; the extension field exists
   184		% only for k >= 1, so that domain condition is made explicit here.
   185		Let $q$ be a prime power and $k \ge 1$ an integer, so that $\F_q$ is a
   186		subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of dimension $k$
   187		over $\F_q$.
   188		Fix a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The bijection
   189		$\kappa_q : \F_{q^k} \to \F_q^k$ associated with this basis is
   190		\[
   191			\kappa_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k\;, \qquad
   192			\text{where } a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i\;.
   193		\]
   194		The map $\kappa_q$ is an isomorphism of $\F_q$-vector spaces; in particular
   195		$\kappa_q(a + b) = \kappa_q(a) + \kappa_q(b)$ for all $a, b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   196		Moreover, multiplication by a fixed element corresponds to a linear map:
   197		for every $a \in \F_{q^k}$ there is a matrix $K_a \in \Mat_k(\F_q)$, the
   198		\emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to $\{e_i\}$}, such that
   199		$\kappa_q(ab) = K_a\, \kappa_q(b)$ for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   200		The map extends coordinatewise to vectors, matrices, and sets: for
   201		$v = (v_1, \dots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$ set
   202		$\kappa_q(v) = (\kappa_q(v_i))_{i=1}^n \in \F_q^{kn}$; for
   203		$M = (M_{i,j}) \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ let
   204		$\chi_q(M) \in \Mat_{mk,nk}(\F_q)$ be the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th
   205		block is $K_{M_{i,j}}$; and for a set $S$ of vectors put
   206		$\kappa_q(S) = \{\kappa_q(v) : v \in S\}$. When $q = p$ is the field
   207		characteristic, the subscript is omitted and we write $\kappa$ and $\chi$.
   208	\end{definition}
   209	
   210	\begin{definition}[Admissible field size]\label{def:admissible-size}
   211		A field size $q$ is \emph{admissible} if $q = 2^k$ for an odd integer $k$.
   212	\end{definition}
   213	
   214	Only fields $\F_{2^k}$ with $k$ odd are used in the analysis of the Pauli basis
   215	test.
   216	
   217	\begin{definition}[Trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$]\label{def:subfield-trace}
   218		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size}
   219		The \emph{trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$} is the map
   220		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   221		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   222			\tr_{q^k \to q} : a \mapsto \Tr(K_a)
   223		\end{equation}
   224		for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $K_a$ is the multiplication table of $a$ with
   225		respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$. The trace is an $\F_q$-linear map from
   226		$\F_{q^k}$ to $\F_q$, and it is independent of the choice of basis, as can
   227		be seen from the equivalent formula
   228		\[
   229			\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   230		\]
   231		For admissible $q = 2^k$ we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q \to 2}$.
   232	\end{definition}
   233	
   234	\begin{definition}[Dual, self-dual, and normal bases]\label{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   235		\uses{def:subfield-trace}
   236		A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', \dots, e_k'\}$ of a basis
   237		$\{e_1, \dots, e_k\}$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$ is a basis such that
   238		$\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for all
   239		$i, j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$. A \emph{self-dual basis} is one equal to its own
   240		dual. If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set
   241		$\{\alpha^{q^j}\}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$, that
   242		basis is called a \emph{normal basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not
   243		exist for every field extension, but for $q = 2$ and odd $k$ a self-dual
   244		normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ always exists; \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}
   245		exhibits one through an explicit construction.
   246	\end{definition}
   247	
   248	\begin{lemma}[Coordinate maps of self-dual bases]\label{lem:downsize_field}
   249		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace,
   250			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   251		Let $q$ be a prime power, $k \ge 1$ an integer, and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual
   252		basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The map $\kappa_q$ corresponding to
   253		$\{e_i\}$ satisfies:
   254		\begin{enumerate}
   255			\item for all $x \in \F_{q^k}$,
   256			      $\kappa_q(x) = \bigl(\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_1), \dots,
   257			      \tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_k)\bigr)$;
   258			\item for all $x, y \in \F_{q^k}$,
   259			      $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \kappa_q(x) \cdot \kappa_q(y)$;
   260			\item for all $M \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in \F_{q^k}^n$,
   261			      $\chi_q(M)\, \kappa_q(v) = \kappa_q(Mv)$.
   262		\end{enumerate}
   263		Items 1 and 2 use self-duality; item 3 holds for an arbitrary basis.
   264	\end{lemma}
   265	\begin{proof}
   266		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   267		For item 1, write $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$, multiply both sides by $e_j$, and
   268		take traces: $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j)
   269		= x_j$ by self-duality. For item 2, expand
   270		$xy = \sum_{i,j} x_i y_j e_i e_j$ and take traces; self-duality retains
   271		exactly the diagonal terms, giving $\sum_i x_i y_i = \kappa_q(x) \cdot
   272		\kappa_q(y)$. For item 3, the $i$-th block of $\kappa_q(Mv)$ equals
   273		$\sum_j \kappa_q(M_{i,j} v_j) = \sum_j K_{M_{i,j}}\, \kappa_q(v_j)$, which
   274		is the $i$-th block row of $\chi_q(M)$ applied to $\kappa_q(v)$.
   275	\end{proof}
   276	
   277	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:one}
   278		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   279		Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ a self-dual normal basis of
   280		$\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$. Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and the
   281		representation $\kappa(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all-ones
   282		vector in $\F_2^k$.
   283	\end{lemma}
   284	\begin{proof}
   285		\uses{lem:downsize_field}
   286		Normality gives $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$ (indices taken cyclically), and
   287		$\tr(b^2) = \tr(b)$ for every $b \in \F_{2^k}$ because squaring permutes the
   288		terms of $\tr(b) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} b^{2^j}$, using $b^{2^k} = b$. Hence all
   289		the values $\tr(e_i)$ coincide. If the common value were $0$, then $\tr$
   290		would vanish identically on $\F_{2^k}$ by linearity; but then item 1 of
   291		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} would give $\kappa(b) =
   292		(\tr(b e_1), \dots, \tr(b e_k)) = 0$ for every $b$, contradicting the
   293		bijectivity of $\kappa$. Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and item 1 of
   294		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} gives
   295		$\kappa(1) = (\tr(e_1), \dots, \tr(e_k)) = (1, \dots, 1)$.
   296	\end{proof}
   297	
   298	\begin{definition}[Binary representation of field elements]\label{def:binary-representation}
   299		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size,
   300			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   301		Let $q = 2^k$ be an admissible field size. For each odd $k$ we fix, once and
   302		for all, a self-dual normal basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   303		$\F_2$ together with its multiplication tables
   304		$\{K_{e_i}\}_{i=1}^k$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis});
   305		the maps $\kappa$ and $\tr$ always refer to this basis. The \emph{binary
   306		representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is the $k$-bit string
   307		$\kappa(a) \in \F_2^k$, the \emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}; the two are
   308		freely identified. Addition of representations is bitwise addition modulo
   309		$2$, and multiplication is determined by the multiplication tables through
   310		\begin{equation}\label{eq:eq-mult}
   311			\kappa(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i\, \kappa(e_i b)
   312			= \sum_{i=1}^k a_i \bigl(K_{e_i}\, \kappa(b)\bigr)\;,
   313		\end{equation}
   314		where $\kappa(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$.
   315	\end{definition}

   317	\section{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   318	% Paper label sec:ld-encoding kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   319	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   320	
   321	\begin{definition}[Individual and total degree]\label{def:polynomials-degree}
   322		\uses{def:polyfunc}
   323		An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   324		\[
   325			f(x_1, \dots, x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m}
   326			c_\alpha\, x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   327		\]
   328		with coefficients $c_\alpha \in \F_q$; the coefficients are uniquely
   329		determined by $f$, since the $q^m$ monomial functions indexed by
   330		$\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m$ span the $q^m$-dimensional space of all
   375	\end{remark}
   376	
   377	The Schwartz--Zippel lemma implies that low-degree polynomials form an
   378	error-correcting code with good distance, the \emph{low-degree code} (a special
   379	case of the generalized Reed--Muller code).
   380	
   381	\begin{definition}[Low-degree encoding]\label{def:low-degree-encoding}
   382		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   383		Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$. For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$
   384		define the $m$-variate multilinear polynomial over $\F_q$
   385		\[
   386			\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)
   387			= \prod_{i : y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i : y_i = 0} (1 - x_i)\;,
   388		\]
   389		identifying $\{0,1\}$ with a subset of $\F_q$. Restricted to the subcube
   390		$\{0,1\}^m$, the polynomial $\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}$ vanishes everywhere except
   391		at $x = y$, where it equals $1$. For $a \in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates
   392		of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ (identifying $\{0,1\}^m$ with
   393		$\{1, \dots, M\}$ by the lexicographic ordering). The \emph{low-degree
   394		encoding of $a$} is the multilinear polynomial $g_a : \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   395		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   396		\begin{equation}\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   397			g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\;.
   398		\end{equation}
   399		For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ one has $g_a(y) = a_y$, and $g_a$ has total
   400		degree at most $m$.
   401	\end{definition}
   402	
   403	\begin{definition}[Indicator vector and linearity of the encoding]\label{def:indicator-vector}
   404		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   405		For $x \in \F_q^m$, the \emph{indicator vector} is
   406		\[
   407			\mathrm{ind}_m(x)
   408			= \bigl(\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\bigr)_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} \in \F_q^M\;.
   409		\]
   410		With this notation the low-degree encoding satisfies, for every
   411		$a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$,
   412		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   413		\begin{equation}\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   414			g_a(x) = a \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(x)\;;
   415		\end{equation}
   416		in particular the map $a \mapsto g_a$ is $\F_q$-linear.
   417	\end{definition}
   418	
   419	Since encodings $g_a$ are multilinear, hence of total degree at most $m$, two
   420	encodings of distinct strings agree on at most an $m/q$ fraction of points of
   421	$\F_q^m$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel}.
   422	
   423	\begin{definition}[Decoding maps]\label{def:decoding-map}
   424		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding}
   425		For $H \subseteq \F_q$, the \emph{decoding map} $\mathrm{Dec}_H$ takes as
   426		input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and returns the vector
   427		$a \in \F_q^M$ defined by: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, set $a_y = g(y)$ if
   428		$g(y) \in H$, and $a_y = 0$ otherwise. For all $a \in H^M$ one has
   429		$\mathrm{Dec}_H(g_a) = a$. We write $\mathrm{Dec}(\cdot)$ for the boolean
   430		decoding map $\mathrm{Dec}_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.
   431	\end{definition}
   432	
   433	\section{Lines}
   434	
   435	The question distributions of the classical low individual degree game and of
   436	the Pauli basis test (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}) sample lines in $\F_q^m$;
   437	we record here the definition of lines and their canonical representatives.
   438	
   439	\begin{definition}[Lines]\label{def:line}
   440		A \emph{line} $\ell$ in $\F_q^m$ specified by a pair
   441		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset
   442		\begin{equation}\label{eq:line-set}
   443			\ell(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m\;.
   444		\end{equation}
   445		The vector $v$ is called a \emph{direction} of $\ell(u,v)$; the case $v = 0$
   446		is explicitly allowed, in which case the line is the singleton $\{u\}$. A
   447		line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate
   448		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   449		vector of $\F_q^m$; such a line is said to be \emph{parallel to the $i$-th
   450		direction}. A line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists
   451		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   452		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).
   453	\end{definition}
   454	
   455	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:line-equiv}
   456		\uses{def:line}
   457		Let $u, v \in \F_q^m$. Then for all $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, we have
   458		$\ell(u,v) = \ell(u',v)$.
   459	\end{proposition}
   460	\begin{proof}
   461		\uses{def:line}
   462		Fix $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, so $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$. Any
   463		$a \in \ell(u,v)$ has the form $a = u + sv = u' + (s - t)v$, so
   464		$\ell(u,v) \subseteq \ell(u',v)$. The symmetric argument gives the reverse
   465		inclusion.
   466	\end{proof}
   467	
   468	Thus, for a fixed direction, a line is an equivalence class of its points: the
   469	pair $(u,v)$ representing it can use any base point on the line. A canonical
   470	representation is obtained as follows.
   471	
   472	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]\label{def:line-representative}
   473		\uses{def:line, def:cl-canonical, prop:line-equiv}
   474		Let $\ell$ be a line in direction $v \neq 0$, and let
   475		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v : \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with
   476		the one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$
   477		(Definition~\ref{def:cl-canonical}). The \emph{canonical representative of
   478		$\ell$} is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   479		\[
   480			u_0 = L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u) \qquad \text{for all } u \in \ell\;.
   481		\]
   482		This is well defined: since the image and kernel of $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ are
   483		complementary, any $u \in \ell$ decomposes uniquely as $u = u_0 + tv$ with
   484		$u_0$ in the image, so $u_0 = u - tv \in \ell$ and
   485		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u_0) = u_0$; moreover any two points of $\ell$ differ by
   486		a multiple of $v$ and therefore have the same image under
   487		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$. A line $\ell = \ell(u,v)$ is henceforth canonically
   488		represented by the pair $(u_0, v)$. (For $v = 0$, where the singleton
   489		$\{u\}$ leaves no independent kernel basis, we take $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_0$ to
   490		be the identity---the canonical linear map with empty kernel basis---so
   491		that $u_0 = u$; the source leaves this case implicit.)
   492	\end{definition}

   494	\section{Quantum registers and EPR states}
   495	% Paper label sec:lin-reg kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   496	\label{sec:lin-reg}
   497	
   498	\begin{definition}[State space of a linear register]\label{def:lin-reg}
   499		\uses{def:complementary}
   500		For a set $V$, we write $\C^V$ for the complex vector space of dimension
   501		$|V|$, endowed with the canonical orthonormal basis
   502		$\{\ket{x}\}_{x \in V}$. A \emph{quantum state on $V$} is a unit vector
   503		$\ket{\psi}_V \in \C^V$. If $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k V_i$ is a direct sum of
   504		subspaces over $\F$, then $\C^V$ is identified with
   505		$\bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{V_i}$ by identifying
   506		$\ket{x_1 \oplus \dots \oplus x_k}$ with
   507		$\ket{x_1} \ot \dots \ot \ket{x_k}$. In particular, a basis $\{e_i\}$ of
   508		$V$ yields the decomposition $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k (\F e_i)$ and hence
   509		$\C^V = \bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{|\F|}$; the factors $\C^{|\F|}$ are called
   510		the \emph{qudits} of $\C^V$.
   511	\end{definition}
   512	
   513	\begin{definition}[EPR state]\label{def:EPR}
   514		\uses{def:lin-reg}
   515		For a linear space $V$ over a finite field $\F$, the \emph{EPR state} on
   516		$\C^V \ot \C^V$ is
   517		\[
   518			\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}_V
   519			= \frac{1}{\sqrt{|V|}} \sum_{x \in V} \ket{x} \ot \ket{x}\;.
   520		\]
   521		We write $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ for $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}_{\F_q}$ and
   522		$\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}$ for $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$.
   523	\end{definition}

   525	\section{Generalized Pauli observables}
   526	% Paper label sec:generalized-pauli kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   527	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
   528	
   529	\begin{definition}[Generalized Pauli observables]\label{def:generalized-pauli}
   530		\uses{def:subfield-trace, def:lin-reg}
   531		Let $p$ be a prime and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/p}$. The \emph{generalized Pauli
   532		observables over $\F_p$} are the unitaries on $\C^{\F_p}$ given by
   533		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-fp}
   534			\sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \F_p} \ket{j + a}\bra{j}
   535			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   536			\sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \F_p} \omega^{bj} \ket{j}\bra{j}
   537		\end{equation}
   538		for $a, b \in \F_p$, with arithmetic over $\F_p$. For $q = p^k$, the
   539		\emph{generalized Pauli observables over $\F_q$} are the unitaries on
   540		$\C^{\F_q}$
   541		\[
   542			\tau^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \F_q} \ket{j + a}\bra{j}
   543			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   544			\tau^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \F_q} \omega^{\tr(bj)} \ket{j}\bra{j}
   545		\]
   546		for $a, b \in \F_q$, where $\tr$ here denotes $\tr_{q \to p}$
   547		(Definition~\ref{def:subfield-trace}); for admissible $q$ this agrees with
   548		the standing shorthand, $p = 2$, and $\omega = -1$, so that all phases are
   549		signs. All the $\tau^X$ operators commute with one another, as do all the
   550		$\tau^Z$ operators. Their common eigenbases consist of the vectors
   551		$\ket{e_W}$, labeled by $e \in \F_q$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
   552		\[
   553			\ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{j \in \F_q}
   554			\omega^{-\tr(ej)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
   555			\ket{e_Z} = \ket{e}\;;
   556		\]
   557		the Fourier transform
   558		\begin{equation}\label{eq:fourier-f}
   559			F = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b \in \F_q}
   560			\omega^{-\tr(ab)} \ket{a}\bra{b}
   561		\end{equation}
   562		maps the computational ($Z$) eigenbasis to the $X$ eigenbasis. We write
   563		$\{\tau^W_e\}_{e \in \F_q}$ for the projective measurement whose elements
   564		are the rank-one projectors onto the vectors of the $W$ eigenbasis. For
   565		systems of $n$ qudits, we write, for $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a \in \F_q^n$,
   566		\[
   567			\tau^W(a) = \tau^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \tau^W(a_n)\;, \qquad
   568			\ket{e_W} = \ket{(e_1)_W} \ot \dots \ot \ket{(e_n)_W}
   569		\]
   570		for $e \in \F_q^n$, with associated rank-one projectors $\tau^W_e$.
   571	\end{definition}
   572	
   573	\begin{lemma}[Product and twisted commutation relations]\label{lem:twisted-commutation}
   574		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   575		Let $q = p^k$, let $n \ge 1$ be an integer, and let $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   576		\begin{enumerate}
   577			\item For all $a, a' \in \F_q$ and $b \in \F_p$,
   578			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
   579				      \tau^W(a)\, \tau^W(a') = \tau^W(a + a')
   580				      \qquad \text{and} \qquad
   581				      \bigl(\tau^W(a)\bigr)^b = \tau^W(ab)\;;
   582			      \end{equation}
   583			      in particular $\bigl(\tau^W(a)\bigr)^p = \Id$, so each
   584			      $\tau^W(a)$ is a unitary with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots
   585			      of unity.
   586			\item For all $a, b \in \F_q^n$,
   587			      % Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   588			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-fq}
   589				      \tau^X(a)\, \tau^Z(b)
   590				      = \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)}\, \tau^Z(b)\, \tau^X(a)\;,
   591			      \end{equation}
   592			      where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i \in \F_q$. The case
   593			      $q = p$, $n = 1$ reads
   594			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-fp}
   595				      \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b)
   596				      = \omega^{-ab}\, \sigma^Z(b)\, \sigma^X(a)
   597				      \qquad \text{for all } a, b \in \F_p\;.
   598			      \end{equation}
   599		\end{enumerate}
   600	\end{lemma}
   601	\begin{proof}
   602		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace}
   603		All identities are verified on computational basis states. For the product
   604		relations with $W = X$, shifting twice by $a'$ and $a$ equals shifting by
   605		$a + a'$; with $W = Z$, the phases $\omega^{\tr(aj)}\omega^{\tr(a'j)}$
   606		combine by $\F_q$-linearity of the trace, and the power relation follows by
   607		iterating. For the scalar twisted commutation,
   608		$\tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)\ket{j} = \omega^{\tr(bj)}\ket{j + a}$, while
   609		$\tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a)\ket{j} = \omega^{\tr(b(j+a))}\ket{j + a} =
   610		\omega^{\tr(ab)}\,\omega^{\tr(bj)}\ket{j + a}$. The multi-qudit relation
   611		follows by applying the scalar relation factor by factor and summing the
   612		exponents, using $\tr(a \cdot b) = \sum_i \tr(a_i b_i)$. For $q = p$ the
   613		trace is the identity map, which gives \eqref{eq:twisted-fp}.
   614	\end{proof}

   616	\begin{lemma}[Fourier cancellation over a subspace]\label{lem:cancellation}
   617		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal, def:subfield-trace}
   618		Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F_q^k$ and let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/p}$, where
   619		$p$ is the characteristic of $\F_q$ and $\tr = \tr_{q \to p}$. For all
   620		$v \notin V^\perp$,
   621		\[
   622			\E_{\bu \sim V}\, \omega^{\tr(\bu \cdot v)} = 0\;,
   623		\]
   624		where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $\bu$ in $V$.
   625	\end{lemma}
   626	\begin{proof}
   627		This is Fact 3.2 of \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Since $v \notin V^\perp$,
   628		the $\F_q$-linear functional $u \mapsto u \cdot v$ is not identically zero
   629		on $V$, hence surjective onto $\F_q$; composing with the nonzero map $\tr$
   630		shows that there is $u_0 \in V$ with $\tr(u_0 \cdot v) \neq 0$. Writing $C$
   631		for the expectation, translation invariance of the uniform distribution on
   632		$V$ gives
   633		$C = \E_{\bu \sim V}\, \omega^{\tr((\bu + u_0) \cdot v)}
   634		= \omega^{\tr(u_0 \cdot v)}\, C$, and $\omega^{\tr(u_0 \cdot v)} \neq 1$
   635		forces $C = 0$.
   636	\end{proof}

   639		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace}

1	\section{Classical and Quantum Low-degree Tests}
     2	\label{sec:ldt}
     3	
     4	In this section we introduce the classical and quantum low individual degree tests, that form the basis of our classical, quantum-sound and quantum PCP constructions. For quantum soundness of the classical test we refer to~\cite{ML20}. For the quantum test, we refer to~\cite{natarajan2018low} and its adaptation to the low individual degree test given in Appendix~\ref{sec:qld-analysis}. 
     5	The protocol in this work combines both of these tests, using the quantum
     6	low individual degree test for question reduction and the classical low individual degree test for
     7	answer reduction.
     8	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier} below introduces the classical test,
     9	and Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier} does the same for the quantum 
    10	test.
    11	Prior to doing this, we introduce the \emph{Magic Square game} in
    12	Section~\ref{sec:ms}, a key subroutine in the quantum test.
    13	
    14	
    15	\subsection{The classical low-degree test}
    16	\label{sec:ld-verifier}
    17	
    18	We begin with a generalization of the classical low-degree test known as the
    19	``simultaneous individual low-degree test''.
    20	We sometimes refer to this as the ``classical low-degree test'' for short.
    21	The low-degree test is used as a subroutine in the Pauli Basis test (see
    22	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) as well as the answer-reduction normal form
    23	verifier (see Section~\ref{sec:ans}).
    24	We describe the test as a nonlocal game in Section~\ref{sec:ld-game} and show
    25	that the question distribution can be implemented as a (typed) conditionally
    26	linear distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL
    27	distributions).
    28	
    29	
    30	\subsubsection{The game}
    31	\label{sec:ld-game}
    32	
    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]
    84	which is a uniformly random line in the affine subspace of $\F^m_q$
    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.
    87	The points player responds with a value $a \in \F_q$, the lines player responds
    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical
    93	parameterization of $\line$).
    94	
    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive
    96	either the same points question, the same axis-parallel lines question, or the
    97	same diagonal lines question.
    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.
    99	
   100	
   101	
   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}

   880	\subsection{The Pauli basis test}
   881	\label{sec:pauli-verifier}
   882	
   883	We introduce the quantum low-degree test of~\cite{natarajan2018low} in the form
   884	of a slight modification to it by~\cite{NW19} known as the \emph{Pauli basis
   885	  test}.
   886	Informally, the quantum low-degree test asks the players to measure a large
   887	number of qubits and return a highly compressed version of the measurement
   888	outcome.
   889	The Pauli basis test simply asks that the players return their uncompressed
   890	measurement outcomes, and it is designed by direct reduction to the quantum
   891	low-degree test.
   892	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-game} we describe the Pauli basis test as a nonlocal
   893	game $\game^\pauli$ and show that its question distribution is implementable via
   894	a CL distribution, as we did with the classical low-degree test in
   895	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   896	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-complexity} we exhibit canonical parameters for the
   897	Pauli basis test and give bounds on the time complexity of executing the test.
   898	
   899	\subsubsection{The game}
   900	\label{sec:qld-game}
   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.
   957

    37	\subsection{Turing machines}
    38	\label{sec:tms}
    39	
    40	Turing machines are a model of computation introduced
    41	in~\cite{turing1937computable}, and play a central role in our modeling of verifiers for nonlocal
    42	games. Here we give an overview of certain aspects of Turing machines that are relevant for
    43	this paper. For an in-depth treatment of Turing machines, we refer the reader to the textbooks of 
    44	Papadimitriou~\cite{Pap94} or Sipser~\cite{sipser2012introduction}.
    45	
    46	The tapes of a Turing machine are infinite one-dimensional arrays of cells that
    47	are indexed by natural numbers.
    48	A \emph{$k$-input} Turing machine $\cal{M}$ has $k$ input tapes, one work tape,
    49	and one output tape. 
    50	Each cell of a tape has symbols taken either from the set $\{0,1\}$ or the blank
    51	symbol $\sqcup$.
    52	At the start of the execution of a Turing machine, the work and output tapes are
    53	initialized to have all blank symbols.
    54	A Turing machine \emph{halts} when it enters a designated halt state.
    55	The \emph{output} of a Turing machine, when it halts, is the binary string that
    56	occupies the longest initial stretch of the output tape that does not have a
    57	blank symbol.
    58	If there are only blank symbols on the output tape, then by convention we say
    59	that the Turing machine's output is $0$.
    60	
    61	Every $k$-input Turing machine $\cal{M}$ computes a (partial) function $f: (\{0,
    62	1\}^*)^k \to \{0,1\}^*$ where the function is only defined on subset $S
    63	\subseteq (\{0,1\}^*)^k$ of inputs $x$ on which $\machine$ halts.
    64	We use $\cal{M}(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_k)$ to denote the output of a $k$-input
    65	Turing machine $\cal{M}$ when $x_i \in \{0,1\}^*$ is written on the $i$-th input
    66	tape for $i \in \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$.
    67	If $\cal{M}$ does not halt on an input $x$, then we define $\cal{M}(x)$ to be
    68	$\bot$.
    69	
    70	
    71	The \emph{time complexity} of a Turing machine $\cal{M}$ on input $x = (x_1,
    72	x_2, \ldots, x_k)$, denoted by $\TIME_{\cal{M},\, x}$, is the number of time
    73	steps that $\cal{M}$ takes on input $x$ before it enters its designated halt
    74	state; if $\cal{M}$ never halts on input $x$, then we define $\TIME_{\cal{M},x}
    75	= \infty$.
    76	
    77	Every Turing machine $\cal{M}$ has a canonical encoding as a bit string $\desc{\cal{M}} \in \{0, 1\}^*$, called
    78	the \emph{canonical description of $\cal{M}$}. The canonical encoding describes the 
    79	finite number of states and transition rules of $\cal{M}$. The details of this 
    80	encoding are not important for this paper; we assume that some ``reasonable'' encoding scheme is
    81	used where the bit length of the encoding is at most some fixed polynomial in the number of 
    82	states. The length of the description
    83	$\desc{\cal{M}}$ is denoted by $|\desc{\cal{M}}|$. 
    84	For every integer $k \in \N$ and every string $\alpha \in \{0, 1\}^*$, the
    85	$k$-input Turing machine described by $\alpha$ is denoted $[\alpha]_k$.
    86	
    87	Throughout this paper we frequently give high-level descriptions of Turing machines in English language, 
    88	rather than explicitly describing them in terms of states and transition functions. In doing so we implicitly assume that all such descriptions can be formally converted into a description in terms of states and transition functions such that there is no hidden blow-up in the complexity of the representation.

    96	\paragraph{Turing machine simulation.} We frequently describe Turing machines as running or simulating other Turing machines as
    97	``subroutines''. We assume that such simulations can be performed with a polynomial overhead in terms of the time complexity. 
    98	For example, suppose $\cal{A}$ is a $1$-input Turing machine that has the following high-level
    99	description: on input $x$ (interpreted as an integer) it runs a $2$-input Turing machine $\cal{B}$ on the input $(x,x^2)$ and obtains an output $y$ (if $\cal{B}$ halts),
   100	and then finally $\cal{A}$ returns the output $y$. We assume that $\cal{A}$ can efficiently simulate the Turing
   101	machine $\cal{B}$, even though $\cal{B}$ 
   102	has a different number of input tapes. This is because every
   103	$k$-input Turing machine $\cal{M}$ can be efficiently simulated 
   104	by a single \emph{tape} Turing machine, as given by the following result~\cite{hartmanis1965computational}.
   105	We assume that there is an unambiguous, binary encoding
   106	$\mathrm{enc}_k(x)$ of $k$-tuples $x \in (\{0,1\}^*)^k$ that is computable in

   111	  01$, $1 \mapsto 10$, and the end of the string $x_i$ is indicated by $00$.}

     4	\subsection{Conditionally linear functions and distributions}
     5	\label{sec:cl}
     6	
     7	We first introduce \emph{conditionally linear functions}, which are used to
     8	specify the question distribution for games considered in the paper in a way
     9	that the question distribution can be ``introspected'', as described in
    10	Section~\ref{sec:introspection}.
    11	Intuitively, a conditionally linear function takes as input an element
    12	$x\in V = \F^n$ for some $n\geq 0$, and applies linear maps $L_j$ sequentially
    13	on $x^{V_j}$ where $V_1,V_2,\ldots $ are a sequence of complementary register
    14	subspaces such that both the linear maps $L_j$ and the subspace $V_j$ for
    15	$j \ge 2$ may depend on the values taken by previous linear maps $L_1(x^{V_1})$,
    16	$L_2(x^{V_2})$, etc.
    17	
    18	In the remainder of the section we use $V$ to denote the linear space $\F^n$ for
    19	some integer $n \geq 0$.
    20	For ease of notation we extensively use the subscript range notation.
    21	For example, if $V_1, V_2, \ldots, V_\ell$ are fixed subspaces of $V$ and $k \in
    22	\{1, 2, \ldots, \ell\}$ we write
    23	\begin{equation*}
    24	  V_{<k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\,1 \le j<k} V_j\;,\quad
    25	  V_{> k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\, \ell\ge j > k} V_j\;,
    26	\end{equation*}
    27	and it is understood that $V_{\le k}$ and $V_{\ge k}$ are identical to
    28	$V_{<k+1}$ and $V_{>k-1}$, respectively.
    29	Moreover, if $V'$ is a register subspace of $V$, $F: V' \to V'$ is a function,
    30	and $x \in V$, we write $x^F$ to denote $F(x^{V'})$.
    31	For example, in the following definition $x^{L_1}$ is used as shorthand notation
    32	for $L_1(x^{V_1})$.
    33	
    34	
    35	\begin{definition}
    36	  \label{def:cl-func}
    37		Let $V$ be $\F^n$ for some $n\geq 0$.
    38	  For all integers $\ell\geq 0$ the collection of \emph{$\ell$-level
    39	    conditionally linear functions} (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is defined
    40	  inductively as follows.
    41	  \begin{enumerate}
    42	  \item There is a single $0$-level conditionally linear function, which is the
    43	    $0$ function on $V$.
    44	
    45	  \item Let $\ell \geq 1$ and suppose the collection of $(\ell-1)$-level
    46	    conditionally linear functions has been defined.
    47	    The collection of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions on $V$ consists
    48	    of all functions $L$ on $V$ that can be expressed in the following form.
    49	    There exist complementary register subspaces $V_1$ and $V_{>1}$ of $V$, a
    50	    linear function $L_1$ on $V_1$, and for all $v \in L_1(V_1)$, an
    51	    $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear function $L_{>1,\, v}$ on $V_{>1}$,
    52	    such that for all $x\in V$,
    53	    \begin{equation*}
    54	      L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}} (x^{V_{>1}})\;.
    55	    \end{equation*}
    56	  \end{enumerate}
    57	\end{definition}
    58	
    59	The concept of conditionally linear functions is simple even though the
    60	notations seem complicated.
    61	It is best understood using an operational definition illustrated in
    62	\cref{fig:cl-functions}.
    63	We give an example of a $2$-level CL function in \cref{ex:cl-function}.
    64	
    65	\begin{remark}
    66	  \label{rk:level-1-is-linear}
    67	  It follows from the above definition that all $1$-level CL functions are linear.
    68	\end{remark}
    69	
    70	\begin{example}\label{ex:cl-function}
    71	Consider $V = \F_{2}^{3}$. Then the following map
    72	\begin{equation*}
    73	  L:(x_{0}, x_{1}, x_{2})
    74	  \mapsto (0, x_{0}x_{2} + x_{1}x_{2} + x_{0},  x_{2})
    75	\end{equation*}
    76	on $V$ is a $2$-level CL function by choosing $V_{1} = \mathrm{span}\{(0,0,1)\}$, $L_{1}$
    77	the identity function on $V_{1}$, $V_{2} = V_{1}^{\perp}$, and
    78	\begin{equation*}
    79	  L_{2,\, x_{2}}: (x_{0}, x_{1}, 0)
    80	  \mapsto (0, x_{0}x_{2} + x_{1}x_{2} + x_{0}, 0),
    81	\end{equation*}
    82	which is linear for all $x_{2} \in \F_{2}$.
    83	Note that intuitively the function $L$ selects either $x_{0}$ or $x_{1}$ in the

     9	\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
    10	 for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeed with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^q)^{\otimes M}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
    11	\begin{enumerate}
    12	    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
    13	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
    14	    \begin{gather*}
    15	        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\tau^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\

    22	$m$ the number of variables, $d$ the degree of the low-degree code,
    23	and $\nqubits=2^m$ is the number of $\ket{\EPR_q}$ states being tested for.

    25	This appendix is structured as follows. First, we establish some preliminary facts and definitions 
    26	in \Cref{sec:qld-prelim}. In the remainder of the appendix, we
    27	show \Cref{thm:pauli-appendix} by showing how to construct a representation of
    28	the Pauli group on the provers' Hilbert space, starting from a
    29	strategy $\strategy$ that succeeds in $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ with
    30	high probability. This is done in several stages: in
    31	\Cref{sec:commutation}, we use the strategy measurements to define a
    32	set of observables that correspond to a subset of the Pauli $X$ and
    33	$Z$ observables, and show that these
    34	approximately satisfy the associated Pauli group relations. In \Cref{sec:expanding},
    35	we adjoin ancillary registers containing EPR states to the provers'
    36	state $\ket{\psi}$, and define a new set of approximately-commuting
    37	observables acting on the expanded state. In \Cref{sec:combining}, we
    38	combine the approximately-commuting observables into a strategy for
    39	the \emph{classical} low-degree test, and in \Cref{sec:apply-ldt}, we
    40	apply the soundness theorem of the classical low-degree test to
    41	construct a single projective measurement that simultaneously measures all of the
    42	approximately-commuting observables. Finally, in
    43	\Cref{sec:separating}, we use this single simultaneous measurement to
    44	construct an exact representation of the Pauli group, show that it
    45	is close to the original strategy observables on the expanded state, and deduce that the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ is a self-test for the strategy $\strategy^\pauli$.

    51	\begin{definition}
    52	Given integer $d,m$ and a prime power $q$ we denote by $\ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ the set of polynomials in $m$ variables
    53	  with \emph{individual} degree at most $d$ in each variable. When the field is clear from context we write $\ideg_{d,m}$. 	
    54		When
    55	  the number of variables is clear from context we
    56	  write $\ideg_d$. We denote by $\deg_{d}$ the set of polynomials with
    57	  \emph{total} degree at most $d$.

    60	Recall the low-degree code defined in \Cref{sec:ld-encoding}, in which vectors $h \in \F_q^\nqubits$ get mapped to polynomials $g_h \in \ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ such that for every $u \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_h(u) = h_u$ where the coordinates of $h$ are indexed by binary strings of length $m$. For $x\in \F_q^m$, recall the definition of the vector $\ind_m(x) \in \F_q^\nqubits$ from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}. Recall also the finite field trace $\tr(\cdot)=\tr_{q\to 2}(\cdot):\F_q\to\F_2$, where $q=2^k$ for odd $k$, defined in Section~\ref{sec:subfields}.

    63	
    64	Call a tuple $\omega = (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt) \in (\F_q^m)^2
    65	\times (\F_q)^2$ \emph{anticommuting} if the quantity 
    66	 \[\gamma\,=\,\tr ((r_\xpt \cdot
    67	\ind_m(u_\xpt)) \cdot (r_\zpt \cdot \ind_m(u_\zpt)))\]
    68	introduced in~\Cref{eq:gamma-value} is not $0$, and \emph{commuting} if $\gamma=0$.
    69	
    70	\begin{fact}
    71	\label{fact:omega-anticomm-prob}
    72		The probability that a tuple $\omega= (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$ sampled uniformly at random from $(\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$
    73		is anti-commuting is at least 
    74		\[
    75			(1 - q^{-m}) \cdot (1 - q^{-1}) \cdot \Big (1 - \frac{md}{q} \Big )  \cdot \frac{1}{2} \geq \Big (1 - \frac{3md}{q} \Big ) \cdot \frac{1}{2}.
    76		\]
    77		The probability that $\omega$ is commuting is also at least $\Big(1 - \frac{3md}{q} \Big ) \cdot \frac{1}{2}$.
    78	\end{fact}

    81		\begin{align*}
    82			\tr( (r_\xpt \cdot \ind_m(u_\xpt)) \cdot (r_\zpt \cdot
    83	                \ind_m(u_\zpt))) &= \tr( r_\xpt r_\zpt (\ind_m(u_\xpt) \cdot \ind_m(u_\zpt))) \\
    84									&= \tr( (r_\xpt r_\zpt) \cdot g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt))\;,
    85		\end{align*}
    86		where $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}$ is a nonzero polynomial in $\ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$.

Since $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}\neq 0$ has total degree at most $md$, by the Schwartz-Zippel lemma the probability that $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt)$ is zero over a uniformly random choice of $u_\zpt$ is at most $md/q$.     96		\E_{x \sim \mu} \bra{\psi} (A^x - B^x)^\dagger (A^x - B^x)
    97	        \ket{\psi}\,\leq\, O(\delta)
    98	      \]

   100	\begin{lemma}
   101	\label{lem:avg-closeness}
   102	Let $\{A^x \}$ and $\{B^x\}$ be operators indexed by some finite set $\mathcal{X}$, and let $\mu$ be a probability distribution over $\mathcal{X}$. Let $\{\alpha_x \}$ be a set of complex numbers such that $|\alpha_x| \leq 1$. Then if $A^x \approx_\delta B^x$ on average over $x$ drawn from $\mu$, then $A \approx_\delta B$, where $A = \E_x \alpha_x A^x$ and $B= \E_x \alpha_x B^x$.
   103	\end{lemma}
   104	\begin{proof}
   105	Expand
   106	\begin{align*}
   107		\Big\| \E_x \alpha_x \big ( A^x - B^x \big) \ket{\psi} \Big\|^2 &\leq \Big( \E_x \norm{ (A^x -B^x) \ket{\psi}} \Big)^2 \\
   108		&\leq \E_x \norm{(A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi}}^2 \\
   109		&\leq \delta\;.
   110	\end{align*}
   111	The first inequality is the triangle inequality and the second inequality is Jensen's inequality. 
   112	\end{proof}

   114	\begin{lemma}
   115	\label{lem:povm-to-obs}
   116	Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a finite set. Let $\{A^x_a \}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ and $\{B^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ be POVMs and let $\{ \alpha_a \}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ be a collection of complex numbers on the unit circle. Let $A^x = \sum_a \alpha_a A^x_a$ and $B^x = \sum_a  \alpha_a B^x_a$. Then 
   117	\[
   118		A^x_a \approx_\delta B^x_a \quad \text{implies} \quad A^x \approx_{\delta'} B^x
   119	\]
   120	for $\delta' = |\mathcal{A}| \cdot \delta$.
   121	\end{lemma}
   122	\begin{proof}
   123	Expand
   124		\begin{align*}
   125			\E_x \norm{(A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi}}^2 &= \E_x \Big\|\sum_a \alpha_a (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi}\Big\|^2 \\
   126			&\leq \E_x \Big( \sum_a \norm{ (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi}} \Big)^2 \\
   127			&\leq \E_x |\mathcal{A}| \cdot \sum_a \norm{ (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi}}^2 \\
   128			&\leq |\mathcal{A}| \cdot \delta\;.

   880	\subsection{The Pauli basis test}
   881	\label{sec:pauli-verifier}
   882	
   883	We introduce the quantum low-degree test of~\cite{natarajan2018low} in the form
   884	of a slight modification to it by~\cite{NW19} known as the \emph{Pauli basis
   885	  test}.
   886	Informally, the quantum low-degree test asks the players to measure a large
   887	number of qubits and return a highly compressed version of the measurement
   888	outcome.
   889	The Pauli basis test simply asks that the players return their uncompressed
   890	measurement outcomes, and it is designed by direct reduction to the quantum
   891	low-degree test.
   892	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-game} we describe the Pauli basis test as a nonlocal
   893	game $\game^\pauli$ and show that its question distribution is implementable via
   894	a CL distribution, as we did with the classical low-degree test in
   895	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   896	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-complexity} we exhibit canonical parameters for the
   897	Pauli basis test and give bounds on the time complexity of executing the test.
   898	
   899	\subsubsection{The game}
   900	\label{sec:qld-game}
   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.

   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).

   964	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   965	We now describe the question distribution of the game $\game^\pauli$, and show
   966	that it is a (typed) CL distribution.
   967	The question types in the game $\game^\pauli$ are
   968	\begin{equation}
   969	  \label{eq:pauli-type}

   980	intuitive description of the question distribution of the Pauli basis test: a

   982	$\game^\pauli$ can be sampled via the following procedure:

  1001	    \chi(s)$, $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v)$, and $u_0 = L^\lnf_{v'}(u_W)$,

@[simp]
theorem weightedSumLinearMap_apply (M : Type*) [AddCommMonoid M] [Module Error M]
    {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → M) :
    𝒟.weightedSumLinearMap M f = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f a :=
  rfl

/-- The scalar average is the weighted finite-sum linear map applied to a scalar
family. -/
theorem avgOver_eq_weightedSumLinearMap {α : Type*}
    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → Error) :
    avgOver 𝒟 f = 𝒟.weightedSumLinearMap Error f := by
  simp [avgOver, smul_eq_mul]

/-- Averaging against a pushed-forward distribution is averaging the pulled-back
function against the original distribution. -/
theorem avgOver_map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (f : β → Error) :
    avgOver (𝒟.map e) f = avgOver 𝒟 (fun a => f (e a)) := by
  simpa [avgOver, smul_eq_mul] using
    Distribution.map_sum_smul (𝒟 := 𝒟) e f

end Distribution

/-- Weighted sum of operators over a distribution's finite support, using the same
`support`/`weight` data as the scalar `avgOver`.

This is a project-local adapter around Mathlib finite sums for the LDT
`Distribution` representation and `Quantum.Op` scalar action, not a replacement for
Mathlib's probability theory APIs. -/
noncomputable def averageOperatorOverDistribution {α : Type*}
    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι :=
  ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f a

namespace Distribution

/-- Operator averaging is the weighted finite-sum linear map applied to an
operator-valued family. -/
theorem averageOperatorOverDistribution_eq_weightedSumLinearMap {α : Type*}
    (𝒟 : Distribution α)
    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (f : α → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) :
    averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 f =
      𝒟.weightedSumLinearMap (MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) f :=
  rfl

/-- Operator-valued averaging against a pushed-forward distribution is
operator-valued averaging of the pulled-back family against the original
distribution. -/
theorem averageOperatorOverDistribution_map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β)
    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (f : β → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) :
    averageOperatorOverDistribution (𝒟.map e) f =
      averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 (fun a => f (e a)) := by
  simpa [averageOperatorOverDistribution] using
    Distribution.map_sum_smul (𝒟 := 𝒟) e f

end Distribution

/-- If two operator-valued families agree pointwise, their averages agree. -/
theorem averageOperatorOverDistribution_congr {α : Type*}
    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (A B : α → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι)
    (h : ∀ a, A a = B a) :
    averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 A = averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 B := by
  exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun a _ => by rw [h a]

/-- Pull a finite outcome sum through an operator-valued average. -/
theorem averageOperatorOverDistribution_sum {α β : Type*} [Fintype β]
    (𝒟 : Distribution α)
    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (f : α → β → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) :
    averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 (fun a => ∑ b : β, f a b) =
      ∑ b : β, averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 (fun a => f a b) := by
  rw [show (fun a => ∑ b : β, f a b) = ∑ b : β, fun a => f a b by
    ext a
    simp]
  simp [Distribution.averageOperatorOverDistribution_eq_weightedSumLinearMap]

/-- Pull a finite-set outcome sum through an operator-valued average. -/
theorem averageOperatorOverDistribution_finset_sum {α β : Type*}
    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (s : Finset β)
    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (f : α → β → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) :
    averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 (fun a => ∑ b ∈ s, f a b) =
      ∑ b ∈ s, averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 (fun a => f a b) := by
  rw [show (fun a => ∑ b ∈ s, f a b) = ∑ b ∈ s, fun a => f a b by
    ext a
    simp]
  simp [Distribution.averageOperatorOverDistribution_eq_weightedSumLinearMap]

/-- Operator averages preserve positivity. -/
theorem averageOperatorOverDistribution_nonneg {α : Type*}
    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι)
    (hf : ∀ a, 0 ≤ f a) :
    0 ≤ averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 f := by
  unfold averageOperatorOverDistribution
  exact Finset.sum_nonneg fun a _ => smul_nonneg (𝒟.nonnegative a) (hf a)

/-- Operator averages preserve pointwise order. -/
theorem averageOperatorOverDistribution_mono {α : Type*}
    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f g : α → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι)
    (hfg : ∀ a, f a ≤ g a) :
    averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 f ≤ averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 g := by
  unfold averageOperatorOverDistribution
  exact Finset.sum_le_sum fun a _ =>
    smul_le_smul_of_nonneg_left (hfg a) (𝒟.nonnegative a)

/-- The average of a constant operator is the total mass times that operator. -/
theorem averageOperatorOverDistribution_const {α : Type*}
    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (A : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) :
    averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 (fun _ : α => A) =
      (∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a) • A := by
  unfold averageOperatorOverDistribution
  rw [Finset.sum_smul]

/-- The average of a constant operator over a probability distribution is that
operator. -/
theorem averageOperatorOverDistribution_const_of_isProbability {α : Type*}
    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (A : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) :
    averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 (fun _ : α => A) = A := by
  rw [averageOperatorOverDistribution_const, h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one]
  simp

/-- An average of effects against a sub-probability distribution is again bounded
above by the identity operator. -/
theorem averageOperatorOverDistribution_le_one_of_weight_sum_le_one {α : Type*}
    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι)
    (h𝒟 : ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a ≤ 1)
    (hf : ∀ a, f a ≤ 1) :
    averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 f ≤ 1 := by
  calc
    averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 f
        ≤ averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 (fun _ : α => 1) := by
          exact averageOperatorOverDistribution_mono 𝒟 f (fun _ : α => 1) hf
    _ = (∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a) • (1 : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) := by
          exact averageOperatorOverDistribution_const 𝒟 1
    _ ≤ (1 : Error) • (1 : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) := by
          exact smul_le_smul_of_nonneg_right h𝒟 zero_le_one
    _ = 1 := by simp

/-- An average of effects against a probability distribution is again bounded
above by the identity operator. -/
theorem averageOperatorOverDistribution_le_one_of_isProbability {α : Type*}
    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability)
    (f : α → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) (hf : ∀ a, f a ≤ 1) :
    averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 f ≤ 1 :=
  averageOperatorOverDistribution_le_one_of_weight_sum_le_one 𝒟 f h𝒟.weight_sum_le_one hf

namespace Distribution

/-- The uniform distribution on a specified finite support.

The stored support is `s`, and the weight of a point is the elementary finite
uniform weight `1 / s.card` on `s` and `0` off `s`.  When the support is empty
this gives the zero sub-probability distribution, matching the convention used
for degenerate filtered supports in the LDT development. -/
noncomputable def uniformOnFinset {α : Type*} (s : Finset α) : Distribution α :=
  letI := Classical.decEq α
  { support := s
    weight := fun a => if a ∈ s then 1 / (s.card : Error) else 0
    nonnegative := fun _ => by
      split_ifs <;> positivity
    outsideSupport := fun _ ha => by
      simp [ha] }

@[simp]
theorem uniformOnFinset_support {α : Type*} (s : Finset α) :
    (uniformOnFinset s).support = s := rfl

@[simp]
theorem uniformOnFinset_weight {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α] (s : Finset α) (a : α) :
    (uniformOnFinset s).weight a =
      if a ∈ s then 1 / (s.card : Error) else 0 := by
  by_cases ha : a ∈ s
  · simp [uniformOnFinset, ha]
  · simp [uniformOnFinset, ha]

/-- A nonempty finite support gives a probability distribution. -/
theorem uniformOnFinset_isProbability {α : Type*} (s : Finset α) (hs : s.Nonempty) :
    (uniformOnFinset s).IsProbability := by
  classical
  dsimp [IsProbability, totalWeight]
  simp_rw [uniformOnFinset_weight]
  have hcard_nat : s.card ≠ 0 := Finset.card_ne_zero.mpr hs
  have hcard : (s.card : Error) ≠ 0 := by
    exact_mod_cast hcard_nat
  have hsum :
      (∑ a ∈ s, if a ∈ s then 1 / (s.card : Error) else 0) =
        ∑ _a ∈ s, 1 / (s.card : Error) := by
    refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    intro a ha
    simp [ha]
  rw [hsum]
  simp [Finset.sum_const, hcard]

/-- The uniform distribution on any finite support is a sub-probability
distribution.  It has mass `1` on nonempty support and mass `0` on empty
support. -/
theorem uniformOnFinset_weight_sum_le_one {α : Type*} (s : Finset α) :
    ∑ a ∈ (uniformOnFinset s).support, (uniformOnFinset s).weight a ≤ 1 := by
  classical
  by_cases hs : s.Nonempty
  · exact (uniformOnFinset_isProbability s hs).weight_sum_le_one
  · have hsempty : s = ∅ := Finset.not_nonempty_iff_eq_empty.mp hs
    simp [hsempty]

/-- The project uniform distribution on a nonempty finite support is Mathlib's
uniform probability mass function on that support. -/
theorem uniformOnFinset_toPMF
    {α : Type*} (s : Finset α) (hs : s.Nonempty) :
    (uniformOnFinset s).toPMF (uniformOnFinset_isProbability s hs) =
      PMF.uniformOfFinset s hs := by
  ext a
  rw [toPMF_apply]
  rw [show (uniformOnFinset s).weight a =
      (PMF.uniformOfFinset s hs a).toReal by
        classical
        by_cases ha : a ∈ s
        · simp [uniformOnFinset_weight, PMF.uniformOfFinset_apply, ha,
            ENNReal.toReal_inv, ENNReal.toReal_natCast]
        · simp [uniformOnFinset_weight, PMF.uniformOfFinset_apply, ha]]
  exact ENNReal.ofReal_toReal ((PMF.uniformOfFinset s hs).apply_ne_top a)

end Distribution

/-- The uniform distribution on a nonempty finite type. -/
noncomputable def uniformDistribution (α : Type*)
    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α] : Distribution α :=
  Distribution.uniformOnFinset Finset.univ

/-- The uniform distribution on a finite type has full support. -/
@[simp]
theorem uniformDistribution_support (α : Type*)
    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α] :
    (uniformDistribution α).support = Finset.univ := rfl

/-- The weights of a uniform distribution sum to exactly `1`. -/
theorem uniformDistribution_weight_sum_eq_one (α : Type*)
    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α] :
    ∑ a ∈ (uniformDistribution α).support, (uniformDistribution α).weight a = 1 := by
  have h : (uniformDistribution α).IsProbability := by
    simpa [uniformDistribution] using
      Distribution.uniformOnFinset_isProbability (Finset.univ : Finset α)
        Finset.univ_nonempty
  exact h.weight_sum_eq_one

/-- The uniform distribution is a genuine probability distribution. -/
theorem uniformDistribution_isProbability (α : Type*)
    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α] :
    (uniformDistribution α).IsProbability := by
  simpa [uniformDistribution] using
    Distribution.uniformOnFinset_isProbability (Finset.univ : Finset α) Finset.univ_nonempty

/-- The weights of a uniform distribution sum to at most `1`. -/
theorem uniformDistribution_weight_sum_le_one (α : Type*)
    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α] :
    ∑ a ∈ (uniformDistribution α).support, (uniformDistribution α).weight a ≤ 1 :=
  le_of_eq (uniformDistribution_weight_sum_eq_one α)

/-- The project uniform distribution on a nonempty finite type is Mathlib's
uniform probability mass function on that type. -/
theorem uniformDistribution_toPMF
    (α : Type*) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α] :
    (uniformDistribution α).toPMF (uniformDistribution_isProbability α) =
      PMF.uniformOfFintype α := by
  simpa [uniformDistribution, PMF.uniformOfFintype] using
    Distribution.uniformOnFinset_toPMF (Finset.univ : Finset α) Finset.univ_nonempty

import Mathlib

/-!
# Basic finite-dimensional matrix operators

This module contains the elementary trace and matrix-algebra facts used by the
finite-dimensional quantum layer.  It introduces the local operator abbreviation
`Op d = Matrix d d ℂ` and keeps the basic trace bookkeeping independent of the
positive-semidefinite order and normalized-trace material.

## References

The declarations in this file are matrix facts for the LDT
formalization of `references/ldt-paper/`.
-/

open scoped BigOperators MatrixOrder Matrix ComplexOrder Matrix.Norms.Elementwise
open WithLp

namespace Matrix

/-! ### Trace bookkeeping -/

/-- Reindexing rows and columns by the same equivalence preserves matrix trace.

This generic matrix lemma is used when moving between equivalent finite index
presentations of the same operator. -/
theorem trace_reindex {α β R : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
    [AddCommMonoid R] (e : α ≃ β) (M : Matrix α α R) :
    Matrix.trace (Matrix.reindex e e M) = Matrix.trace M := by
  classical
  simp only [Matrix.trace, Matrix.diag_apply, Matrix.reindex_apply]
  rw [← e.symm.sum_comp (fun i : α => M i i)]
  rfl

/-! ### Linear matrix maps -/

/-- Taking a submatrix is linear in the ambient matrix.

This packages the entrywise linearity of `Matrix.submatrix` in the same style
as Mathlib's block-diagonal additive and linear maps. -/
def submatrixLinearMap (R : Type*) {m n m' n' α : Type*}
    [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid α] [Module R α]
    (row : m' → m) (col : n' → n) :
    Matrix m n α →ₗ[R] Matrix m' n' α where
  toFun := fun A => Matrix.submatrix A row col
  map_add' := by
    intro A B
    ext i j
    rfl
  map_smul' := by
    intro c A
    ext i j
    rfl

@[simp]
theorem submatrixLinearMap_apply (R : Type*) {m n m' n' α : Type*}
    [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid α] [Module R α]
    (row : m' → m) (col : n' → n) (A : Matrix m n α) :
    Matrix.submatrixLinearMap R row col A = Matrix.submatrix A row col :=
  rfl

/-- The trace pairing of two block-diagonal matrices is the sum of the trace
pairings of the corresponding diagonal blocks. -/
theorem trace_blockDiagonal_mul {o m R : Type*}
    [Fintype o] [DecidableEq o] [Fintype m] [NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring R]
    (B D : o → Matrix m m R) :
    Matrix.trace (Matrix.blockDiagonal B * Matrix.blockDiagonal D) =
      ∑ b : o, Matrix.trace (B b * D b) := by
  rw [← Matrix.blockDiagonal_mul B D, Matrix.trace_blockDiagonal]

end Matrix

namespace MIPStarRE.Quantum

/-! ### Basic operator type -/

/-- Square complex matrices as the finite-dimensional operator algebra. -/
abbrev Op (d : Type*) := Matrix d d ℂ

/-! ### Kronecker product bookkeeping -/

/-- Kronecker product is additive in the right factor, rewritten for subtraction. -/
theorem kronecker_sub_right
    {d₁ d₂ : Type*} {A : Op d₁} {B₁ B₂ : Op d₂} :
    Matrix.kronecker A B₁ - Matrix.kronecker A B₂ =
      Matrix.kronecker A (B₁ - B₂) := by
  have hneg : Matrix.kronecker A (-B₂) = -Matrix.kronecker A B₂ := by
    simpa using (Matrix.kronecker_smul (-1 : ℂ) A B₂)
  calc
    Matrix.kronecker A B₁ - Matrix.kronecker A B₂
        = Matrix.kronecker A B₁ + Matrix.kronecker A (-B₂) := by
            rw [hneg]
            simp [sub_eq_add_neg]
    _ = Matrix.kronecker A (B₁ - B₂) := by
          simpa [sub_eq_add_neg] using (Matrix.kronecker_add A B₁ (-B₂)).symm

/-- Kronecker product is additive in the left factor, rewritten for subtraction. -/
theorem kronecker_sub_left
    {d₁ d₂ : Type*} {A₁ A₂ : Op d₁} {B : Op d₂} :
    Matrix.kronecker A₁ B - Matrix.kronecker A₂ B =
      Matrix.kronecker (A₁ - A₂) B := by
  have hneg : Matrix.kronecker (-A₂) B = -Matrix.kronecker A₂ B := by
    simpa using (Matrix.smul_kronecker (-1 : ℂ) A₂ B)
  calc
    Matrix.kronecker A₁ B - Matrix.kronecker A₂ B
        = Matrix.kronecker A₁ B + Matrix.kronecker (-A₂) B := by
            rw [hneg]
            simp [sub_eq_add_neg]
    _ = Matrix.kronecker (A₁ - A₂) B := by
          simpa [sub_eq_add_neg] using (Matrix.add_kronecker A₁ (-A₂) B).symm

end MIPStarRE.Quantum
